{{Short description|American Christian hymn by Robert Lowry}} {{For|the Falling Skies episode|Shall We Gather at the River (Falling Skies)}} {{sources|date = April 2025}} {{Infobox musical composition | name = Shall We Gather at the River? | type = | image = Robert_Lowry.JPG | alt = | caption = Robert Lowry | translation = | native_name = | native_name_lang = | composer = [[Robert Lowry (hymn writer)|Robert Lowry]] | genre = [[Hymn]] | occasion = | text = | language = | written = 1864 | published = 1865 | publisher = [[American Tract Society]] | based_on = {{Sourcetext|source=Bible|version=King James|book=Revelation|chapter=22|verse=1}} | meter = 8.7.8.7 with refrain | melody = "Hanson Place" | composed = | misc = }} '''"Shall We Gather at the River?"''' or simply '''"At the River"''' are the popular names for the [[Traditional music|traditional]] [[Christianity|Christian]] [[hymn]] originally titled "Beautiful River" and subsequently titled '''"Hanson Place,"''' written by [[United States|American]] [[poet]] and [[gospel music]] composer [[Robert Lowry hymn writer|Robert Lowry]] (1826–1899). It was written in 1864 and is now in the [[Public domain music|public domain]]. The title "Hanson Place" is a reference to the original [[Hanson Place Seventh Day Adventist Church|Hanson Place Baptist Church in Brooklyn]], where Lowry, as a [[Baptists|Baptist]] minister, sometimes served. The original building now houses a different denomination. The music is in the [[key of D]] and uses an 8.7.8.7 R [[Meter (music)|meter]]. An arrangement was also composed by [[Charles Ives]] and titles "At The River." A later arrangement is included in [[Aaron Copland]]'s ''[[Old American Songs]]'' (1952) in addition to being used by German composer [https://www.nachschlage.net/search/kdg/Anton+Plate/816.html Anton Plate] in 'At The River' (2003), and by American wind band composer [[David Maslanka]] in his Symphony No. 9 (2011). The song was sung live at the 1980 funeral of American Supreme Court Justice [[William O. Douglas]]. The Charles Ives version of the hymn was arranged, fully orchestrated for jazz orchestra and recorded the 2014 album ''[[Mists: Charles Ives for Jazz Orchestra]].''
There have been many recordings of the hymn including those by [[Patti Page]], [[Burl Ives]] and [[Willie Nelson]]. {{cite web |title=secondhandsongs.com |url=https://secondhandsongs.com/work/155908/versions#nav-entity |website=secondhandsongs.com |access-date=April 23, 2021}} == Lyrics == The song's lyrics refer to the Christian concept of the anticipation of restoration and reward, and reference the motifs found at {{bibleverse||Revelation|22:1-2|31}} - a crystal clear river with water of life, issuing from the throne of heaven, all presented by an angel of God. It also brings to mind Acts 16:13, where Paul found women gathered by the river outside the city gates of Phillipi. It was one of director [[John Ford]]'s favorite hymns, and he featured it in many of his most famous films. The melody is used satirically in ''[[Stagecoach (1939 film)|Stagecoach]]'' (1939), underscoring the early scene in which [[Claire Trevor]]'s character, Dallas, is run out of town “by the ladies of the Law and Order League.” It also appears in Ford's ''[[Tobacco Road (film)|Tobacco Road]]'' (1941), ''[[My Darling Clementine]]'' (1946), ''[[3 Godfathers|Three Godfathers]]'' (1948), ''[[Wagon Master]]'' (1950), twice in ''[[The Searchers (film)|The Searchers]]'' (1956), and ''[[7 Women]]'' (1966). The song is also heard in [[Gene Fowler, Jr.]]'s ''[[The Oregon Trail (1959 film)|The Oregon Trail]]'' (1959) and in [[Elliot Silverstein]]'s ''[[Cat Ballou]]'' (1965). It was used in the [[Sam Peckinpah]] films ''[[Major Dundee]]'' (1965) and also ''[[The Wild Bunch]]'' (1969) where it was employed as ironic counterpoint during an onscreen massacre. It was similarly put to use in such dark, late-period Westerns as 1968's ''[[Hang 'Em High]]'' and 1972's ''[[Jeremiah Johnson (film)|Jeremiah Johnson]]''.Silva, Robert. {{cite web |url=http://blogs.amctv.com/future-of-classic/2009/01/hang-em-high-hymn.php |title=AMC - Blogs - Future of Classic - in John Ford's West, a Methodist Hymn Starts Somber, then Inspires Sarcasm |accessdate=2009-02-02 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20090116185636/http://blogs.amctv.com/future-of-classic/2009/01/hang-em-high-hymn.php |archivedate=2009-01-16 }} Future of Classic, 2009-01-10. Retrieved on 2009-02-02 The song was used in [[Gore Verbinski]]'s infamous 2013 pastiche western, ''[[The Lone Ranger (2013 film)|The Lone Ranger]].'' ===In other films=== It features prominently in [[David Lean]]'s romantic comedy ''[[Hobson's Choice (1954 film)|Hobson's Choice]]'' (1954) and in [[Richard Brooks]]'s drama ''[[Elmer Gantry (film)|Elmer Gantry]]'' (1960). A [[Caricature|caricatural]] vocal rendition of the song (with new [[Revival meeting|revival-style]] lyrics) is used for both a car chase and the end credits of [[Howard Morris]]' [[Heist film|caper]] comedy, ''[[Who's Minding the Mint?]]'' (1967). It is also included in the film adaptation of [[The Handmaid's Tale (film)]]. Part of the hymn was sung in the Academy Award-winning period film, ''[[Trip to Bountiful]]'' (1985). The hymn is a primary musical theme for schlock film ''[[Tromeo and Juliet]]'' (1996), credited on the soundtrack as ''Yes, We'll Gather at the River''.Amazon website. [https://www.amazon.com/dp/B000001J7C] Retrieved on 2010-06-05 The title "[[Shall We Gather at the River (Falling Skies)|Shall We Gather at the River]]" is used as the name of a second season episode of ''[[Falling Skies]]''. The hymn opens [[Richard Rossi]]'s 1920s period piece drama ''Aimee Semple McPherson''.{{cite news|last1=Gilbert|first1=Ryan|title=Hallelujah! How Faith Healer Aimee Semple McPherson Inspired the Rip-Roaring New Musical Scandalous|url=http://www.broadway.com/buzz/165228/hallelujah-how-faith-healer-aimee-semple-mcpherson-inspired-the-rip-roaring-new-musical-scandalous/|publisher=Broadway Buzz|date=November 5, 2012}}{{cite news|last1=Wooding|first1=Dan|title=Maverick Minister Richard Rossi Goes Hollywood|url=http://www.sloppynoodle.com/wp/maverick-minister-richard-rossi-goes-hollywood/|accessdate=January 28, 2016|agency=Sloppy Noodle Inc.|publisher=Assist News Service|date=February 5, 2011}} ==International use== In Sweden, the 1876 hymn to the same melody ''O, hur saligt att få vandra'' ("O, how blessed it is to walk") became one of the most popular songs of the widespread [[Swedish Evangelical Mission|Swedish revivalist movement]]. A [[Snapsvisa|drinking song]] to the same melody, ''Jag har aldrig vart på snusen'' ("I've never been on [[snus]]"), partly mocking the religious message of the Swedish original, is one of the most popular drinking songs at Swedish universities.{{citation needed|date=January 2013}} In Germany, the melody of the hymn became a well-known christmas carol named ''Welchen Jubel, welche Freude'' ("What rejoice, o what a joy") with the lyrics of {{ill|Ernst Gebhardt|de}} (1832–1899).published in ''Frohe Botschaft in Liedern'' - song no. 17 (page 20) [https://archive.org/details/frohebotschaftin00gebh_0/page/20] In 1937, the tune was adopted in Japan to a popular [[enka]] song ''Tabakoya no Musume'' ({{ill|タバコやの娘|ja}}, "The Girl at the [[Tobacconist]]"). This enka song was soon parodied into juvenile song about the testicles of the [[Japanese raccoon dog|tanuki]] (たんたんたぬき), which goes, "Tan-tan-tanuki's testicles: there isn't any wind, but [they still go] swing swing swing". The parodied version of the song remain popular among Japanese children and adults to this day. "Tabakoya no Musume" later formed the basis of the [[Bic Camera]] jingle.{{cite web |url=https://www.worldfolksong.com/popular/bic-camera.html |title=ビックカメラの歌 CMソング 各店舗の歌詞 |website=World Folk Song |access-date=January 17, 2024}} The [[University of Antioquia]] in [[Medellin, Colombia]] uses the same melody in its official song.University of Antioquia website [http://www.udea.edu.co/wps/portal/udea/web/inicio/institucional/quienes-somos/contenido/asmenulateral/simbolos] (''Spanish'') Retrieved on 2017-07-17 The British band [[Groove Armada]]'s single "[[At the River]]" features a trombone part derived from "Shall We Gather at the River?", played by band member [[Andy Cato]].{{cite web |url=https://www.theguardian.com/music/2018/nov/20/groove-armada-how-we-made-at-the-river-tom-findlay-andy-cato |title=Groove Armada: how we made At the River |last=Simpson |first=Dave |date=20 November 2018 |website=[[theguardian.com]] |access-date=29 November 2018}} ==References== {{reflist}} ==External links== *[http://library.timelesstruths.org/music/Shall_We_Gather_at_the_River/ Lyrics] {{Robert Lowry}} {{Authority control}} [[Category:American Christian hymns]] [[Category:1864 songs]] [[Category:19th-century hymns]] [[Category:Protestant hymns]] [[Category:Hymns by Robert Lowry]]
